name: Kota
script: Tamil script; Latin/IPA in academic literature
lead: Kota (endonym: Kōv Māt) is a Critically Endangered South Dravidian language spoken by the indigenous Kota community across seven settlements (kōkāl) in the Nilgiri Hills of Tamil Nadu, India.[1][2] Together with Toda, it forms the Toda–Kota subgroup of South Dravidian.[3]
history:
The Kota community historically inhabited seven villages in the Nilgiri plateau—including Kollimalai, Porthimund, Kotagiri (Aggal), Kil-Kotagiri, Trichigadi, Sholur, and Gudalur—functioning traditionally as blacksmiths, potters, carpenters, and ceremonial musicians within the Nilgiri inter-tribal system.[1][4]

M. B. Emeneau published a four-volume collection of Kota narratives and a grammatical sketch between 1944 and 1946.[1] The speaker population resides in seven villages and numbers under 1,000 individuals, placing Kota in UNESCO's Critically Endangered category.[2]
phonology: Kota retains a five-vowel quality system (/i, e, a, o, u/) with phonemic vowel length (10 vowels total).[1][3] Unlike Toda, Kota did not develop front rounded vowels, though it experienced unaccented vowel syncope that created dense consonant clusters.[3] Its consonant system contrasts dental, alveolar, and retroflex stops (/t̪, d̪/, /t, d/, /ʈ, ɖ/).[1]
syntax: Kota uses Subject–Object–Verb (SOV) word order.[1] Nouns inflect on an oblique stem for accusative (-n), dative (-k), and locative (-l). Verbs mark past and non-past stems via suffixal alternation, followed by pronominal endings.[1]

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Pronouns & Kinship
lessons.intro: Personal pronouns and core kinship terms from Emeneau (1944: 15–28) and DEDR.<sup>[1][5]</sup>

quiz.q: How does Kota distinguish 'he' and 'she' in the third-person singular?
quiz.a: avn (/avn/, 'he') with masculine suffix -n versus avḷ (/avɭ/, 'she') with feminine suffix -ḷ.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Basic Nouns & Numerals
lessons.intro: Core nouns demonstrating syncope of second-syllable vowels compared to Proto-Dravidian.<sup>[3][5]</sup>

quiz.q: What phonological change does Kota marm ('tree') show relative to Proto-Dravidian *maram?
quiz.a: Loss (syncope) of the unaccented second-syllable short vowel /a/.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Verbal Stems (S1 & S2)
lessons.intro: Every Kota verb has a primary stem (S1) and a secondary past/participial stem (S2).<sup>[1]</sup>

quiz.q: What is the secondary (past) stem of vār- ('to come')?
Which suffix marks the third-person singular masculine subject on uḍ-t-ān?
